result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, a reporter virus encoding a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the cell surface that enables antibody-free magnetic cell sorting (AFMACS) of infected cells. The optimal construct (pNL4-3-ΔEnv-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR) expressed the marker early in infection and achieved ≥90% purity with ≤10% loss in both CEM-T4s and primary CD4+ T cells.
evaluation: All three reviewers praised the technical innovation of HIV-AFMACS. Reviewer 2 specifically highlighted 'the technical innovation' and 'the emphasis on primary cells' as strengths. Reviewer 3 stated the study is 'compelling, appropriately controlled' with no concerns raised about the AFMACS methodology itself. The editors noted all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set using primary CD4+ T cells' and found it 'technically innovative.'

result: Using HIV-AFMACS, the authors quantitated approximately 9000 cellular proteins across multiple donors in primary CD4+ T cells, generating the first high-coverage proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells. The depth of coverage reduced quantitation variability and the high purity (>90% infected) maximized effect sizes, resulting in high signal-to-noise ratios.
evaluation: Reviewers unanimously praised the dataset quality and scope. Reviewer 1 called it 'the largest data set in using primary CD4+ T cells to-date' and 'technically sound.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the depth and stringency of the mass spec data obtained' and noted 'the interactive spreadsheet that provides an easy-to-access and expansive resource.' The editors stated all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set' and that it provides 'an easy-to-access resource for the community.'

result: Among 650 HIV-dependent protein changes (q<0.05), known accessory protein-dependent changes characterized in T cell lines accounted for 297/650 (46%) of proteins regulated in primary T cells, including 175/299 (59%) of decreased proteins. Accessory proteins (Vpr, Vif, Nef, Vpu) account for much of the proteomic remodeling, with pathways including DNA damage response/cell cycle (Vpr), cytidine deamination/PP2A activity (Vif), and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef).
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings without challenge. Reviewer 1 noted 'over half of the 600+ changes were dependent on Vpr and Vif/Nef/Vpu' as a key observation. Reviewer 3 stated the study is 'appropriately controlled' and the results are 'of significant interest to the community.' No reviewer questioned the identification or quantification of accessory protein effects.

result: The authors identified novel Vif-dependent targets DPH7 and FMR1 in primary T cells. Both proteins showed profound Vif-dependent depletion confirmed by proteomics in CEM-T4s and primary cells, and validated by immunoblot in cells infected with WT (but not ΔVif) virus and in cells transduced with Vif alone. Together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors, these account for all significant Vif-dependent changes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 expressed concern about 'novelty and overlap with prior and parallel work' and noted 'the functional significance of these interactions is unclear.' Reviewer 2 stated 'there is rather limited validation of new or interesting hits and no characterization of why they (in particular the highlighted factors DPH7 and FMR1) are affected by HIV or the roles they might play in viral or cellular biology.' While the depletion data are accepted, the biological significance remains questioned.

result: 192/650 (30%) proteins regulated by HIV in primary T cells were either not detected or not significantly regulated in CEM-T4s, including ARID5A and PTPN22. These proteins were consistently depleted across all donors (fold change >2) and validated by immunoblot. Proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 praised 'the emphasis on primary cells' as a strength and noted the validation of ARID5A and PTPN22 'using immunoblot.' Reviewer 1 acknowledged these as 'novel cellular factors' though questioned their functional significance. Reviewer 3 found the study 'compelling' with results 'of significant interest to the community.' The identification and validation of primary cell-specific targets was accepted, though functional characterization was noted as limited.

result: Control experiments showed that expression of SBP-ΔLNGFR as a transgene or in lentiviral vectors caused minimal proteomic perturbations. Only 37/8518 (0.4%) proteins were significantly perturbed by control lentivectors, and only 1/650 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) was also regulated by control vectors. No Tat-dependent changes were identified despite robust LTR transactivation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised a critical concern: 'the authors did not include an evaluation of whether the expression of SBP-LNGFR and its display on the cell surface causes any changes in expression of cellular proteins, as an important negative control.' While the authors present control data (C65-C68), Reviewer 2 specifically requested evaluation of 'whether or not the potential effects of LNGFR overexpression and bead binding can truly be disregarded.' This suggests the control experiments may not fully address potential artifacts.

result: Time-course analysis revealed T cell activation caused extensive proteomic remodeling (29% of proteins changed >2-fold). Known restriction factors showed expected patterns: tetherin was upregulated by activation then depleted in infected cells (Vpu target), while SAMHD1 was depleted by activation independent of infection. Temporal profiling distinguished substrates of different accessory proteins based on characteristic kinetics.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 found the study 'compelling, appropriately controlled' with no specific concerns about the temporal analysis. Reviewer 1 called it 'technically sound.' The temporal profiling approach builds on the authors' previous validated methodology (C12), and reviewers raised no objections to these findings. Reviewer 3's question about T cell activation (point 7) sought discussion rather than challenging the data.

result: Vpr-dependent changes from CEM-T4s were recapitulated in primary T cells, with 33 newly described Vpr substrates quantitated and 32 decreased in abundance. ARID5A and PTPN22 likely represent novel Vpr substrates based on temporal patterns, consistent with ARID5B being a conserved Vpr target.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 noted this represents 'overlap with prior and parallel work' citing 'a sister paper (Greenwood, 2018) that describes the Vpr downregulated proteome.' However, the validation of these targets in primary cells (the natural target) was not challenged. Reviewer 3 stated results are 'of significant interest to the community' without raising concerns about the Vpr findings.

result: Marked increases in proteins associated with lipid and sterol metabolism were observed in HIV-infected cells. Similar effects have been reported in T cell lines at the transcriptional level and attributed to Nef expression, and several proteins in these pathways are indirectly regulated by Vpr.
evaluation: No reviewer challenged these findings. The lipid metabolism changes are presented as confirmatory of previous transcriptional studies (C61) and consistent with known Vpr effects (C62). Reviewers accepted these observations without comment, treating them as supporting rather than novel findings.

result: Compared to previous studies, this work provides superior coverage. Previous temporal proteomic analyses had limited coverage (<2000 proteins) and did not detect known targets. A recent study (Kuo et al. 2018) quantitated 7761 proteins but 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified here were obscured in that study, including ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7 and 19/51 known accessory protein substrates.
evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted the superior quality of this dataset. Reviewer 1 acknowledged it as 'the largest data set in using primary CD4+ T cells to-date.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the depth and stringency of the mass spec data obtained.' The editors noted all reviewers 'were impressed with the magnitude of your data set.' The comparison to previous studies was not challenged.

result: The authors used Env-deficient proviral backbone with VSVg pseudotyping to enhance titers, avoid Env-dependent cytotoxicity, enable synchronous infections, and bypass co-receptor-dependent targeting. VSVg redirects entry to an endocytic pathway and may abrogate Env-dependent signaling. The absence of Env-CD4/co-receptor interactions may have resulted in underestimation of proteomic changes (false negatives).
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised significant concerns: 'it is unfortunate that ΔEnv viruses were chosen for the analysis considering the large impact Env-CD4/CoR binding can have on primary T cell responses' and 'it seems reasonable that their viruses could have been pseudotyped with wild-type Envelope proteins instead of VSV-G.' Reviewer 2 requested 'further discussion of this issue' and noted it would have been 'even more compelling to compare R5 vs. X4 or TF to non-TF glycoproteins.' While the authors acknowledge potential false negatives (C110), the experimental design choice is questioned.

result: AFMACS-based selection offers advantages over conventional methods: it is fast, simple, scalable, antibody-free, and selected cells are released from beads with biotin. Conventional antibody-based methods risk altering cell behavior through receptor cross-linking or bead internalization.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the technical advantages of AFMACS. Reviewer 2 noted 'the technical innovation' as a strength. However, Reviewer 2 also stated 'the authors should also explain the limitations of AFMACS-selection more thoroughly,' suggesting the discussion of advantages should be balanced with limitations. The method's advantages are accepted but may be overstated without adequate discussion of limitations.
